blocks.title: Crystal lattice and crystalline solid
blocks.text: The regular arrangement of ions, atoms or molecules in three-dimensional space is the crystal lattice. Solids with definite, regular three-dimensional geometric shapes are crystalline solids, for example diamond, sodium chloride and ice.

items: Geometrical shape: every crystalline solid has a definite, distinctive geometrical shape because of the definite and orderly arrangement of its atoms, ions or molecules in three-dimensional space. For a given crystal the interfacial angles at which the surfaces meet are always the same whatever shape it is grown in, and the faces and angles remain characteristic even when the material is ground to a fine powder.
Melting point: crystalline solids have sharp melting points and can be identified by them.

Cleavage planes: when crystalline solids break they do so along definite planes, the cleavage planes, which are inclined to one another at a particular angle for a given solid; the angle varies from one solid to another.

Growing a crystal: a saturated or supersaturated solution of a crystalline material in a suitable solvent gives the same type of crystals by arranging its atoms, ions or molecules, through the growth of crystals, by slow evaporation of the solvent or by seeding the saturated solution. The solubility of sodium thiosulfate Na2S2O3 in water is 231 g per 100 cm3 at 100 degrees C and 50 g per 100 cm3 at room temperature; a solution saturated at 100 degrees C and cooled slowly grows no crystals, because the supersaturated solution is not in equilibrium with the solid, but if a small crystal of Na2S2O3 is added, crystallization happens rapidly.

Habit of a crystal: the shape in which a crystal usually grows is its habit. If the growing conditions are maintained the shape always stays the same; if they change the shape may change, for example a cubic crystal of NaCl becomes needle-like when 10 per cent urea is present in its solution as an impurity.
